title: A Full-Spectrum Theory of Moiré Superlattices
authors: Tong Liu, X. R. Wang, Jiansheng Wu
abstract: Conventional theoretical descriptions of moiré superlattices, epitomized by the Bistritzer--MacDonald continuum model, are fundamentally constrained by low-energy Dirac cone approximations and first-shell interlayer coupling truncations. While successful for small-angle twisted bilayer graphene near charge neutrality, these frameworks fail to provide universal analytical solutions for strained lattices, high-energy band behaviors, or arbitrary commensurate geometries. Here, we establish a unified, approximation-free analytical formalism for generalized moiré systems based on three pillars: (i) a rigorous two-dimensional-to-one-dimensional supercell cyclic mapping, (ii) exact block-circulant diagonalization of intralayer Hamiltonians, and (iii) quasi-degenerate Löwdin perturbation theory centered on arbitrary energy degeneracy points across the full spectrum. Unlike traditional schemes anchored to the Dirac point, our approach enables systematic perturbative expansions around any band crossing, unifying the characterization of low-energy flat bands with high-energy degeneracies. We demonstrate that this framework perfectly recovers the Bistritzer--MacDonald model in the low-energy limit while extending its reach to heterostrained systems and high-energy regimes. By incorporating high-order interlayer coupling shells, we reveal an intrinsic scale self-similarity in moiré lattices and predict the emergence of higher-order magic angles and tunable flat bands driven by secondary degeneracies. This work eliminates the long-standing lack of universal analytical tools for diverse moiré platforms, providing a full-spectrum theoretical foundation for band engineering and the exploration of exotic correlated and topological states in van der Waals heterostructures.
summary: This paper introduces a comprehensive, approximation-free theoretical formalism for analyzing moiré superlattices, overcoming the limitations of existing low-energy models. By employing a combination of advanced diagonalization and perturbation theory, the authors map out the entire electronic band structure. This work provides a universal tool for band engineering and exploring exotic correlated states in van der Waals heterostructures.
main_problem: Conventional theoretical models for moiré superlattices are limited by low-energy approximations and truncated interlayer couplings, failing to describe high-energy or strained lattice behaviors universally.
main_result: The authors establish a unified, approximation-free analytical formalism that extends beyond low-energy Dirac points to characterize the full spectrum of moiré systems.
method: The approach combines a rigorous 2D-to-1D supercell mapping, exact block-circulant diagonalization of intralayer Hamiltonians, and quasi-degenerate Löwdin perturbation theory.
model_or_system: The system studied is the moiré superlattice formed by stacking van der Waals materials, modeled by a general Hamiltonian $\mathbf{H}_M$ involving intralayer and interlayer hopping terms.
key_observables: Full energy spectrum, band crossings, flat bands, and the emergence of higher-order magic angles.
important_parameters: The method is applicable across the entire energy spectrum, allowing systematic expansion around any band crossing, not just the Dirac point.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes the ability to perform the supercell mapping and that the Hamiltonian can be systematically decomposed into block-circulant forms.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the supercell structure and the mathematical formulation of the effective Hamiltonian derived from the block diagonalization process.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the limitations of existing models to introducing the three-pillar formalism, demonstrating its application to recover known models while extending to general, high-energy, and strained regimes.
why_interesting: The development of a universal, full-spectrum theoretical tool for moiré systems provides a powerful framework for engineering correlated electronic states, which is highly relevant for understanding emergent quantum phenomena in heterostructures.
